title: 31. Automation, Cron & Reliable Scripts
content:
# 31. Automation, Cron & Reliable Scripts

Automation turns a manual operation into something repeatable. Reliable automation is explicit about environment, paths, errors, locking, logging, and idempotency.

## Learning goals

By the end of this module, you should be able to:

- write scripts that behave consistently outside your interactive shell;
- schedule jobs with cron or systemd timers;
- prevent overlapping runs;
- make automation idempotent where possible;
- capture logs and failures for later diagnosis.

## Non-interactive environments

Scheduled jobs do not inherit your normal interactive setup. Use absolute paths or define `PATH` explicitly:

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
PATH=/usr/local/sbin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/sbin:/usr/bin:/sbin:/bin
```

Do not depend on aliases, prompt configuration, current directory, or manually exported variables.

## Idempotency

An idempotent script can run more than once without causing duplicate damage. Prefer operations like "ensure this directory exists" over "blindly append this line".

```bash
mkdir -p /var/backups/app
```

For file edits, write to a temporary file and move it into place only after successful generation.

## Locking

Prevent overlapping runs when the job touches shared resources:

```bash
flock -n /tmp/app-backup.lock /usr/local/bin/app-backup
```

Without locking, a slow previous run can collide with the next scheduled run.

## Logging

Redirect output deliberately:

```cron
15 * * * * /usr/local/bin/app-check >>/var/log/app-check.log 2>&1
```

For systemd timers, prefer journal logging through the service unit. Logs should include enough context to debug failures without rerunning the job manually.

## Cron basics

```cron
# minute hour day-of-month month day-of-week command
*/5 * * * * /usr/local/bin/health-check
```

Cron syntax is compact and easy to misread. Always document time zone assumptions and test commands outside cron first.

## systemd timers

Timers provide better logs and dependency handling than cron on systemd systems:

```bash
systemctl list-timers
systemctl status cleanup.timer
```

Use timers when jobs need service dependencies, missed-run behavior, or standard `systemctl` management.

## Failure behavior

A useful automation failure tells you what failed, where, and what action is needed. Silent failure is worse than no automation.

## Practice

Create a script that checks a local HTTP endpoint, writes a timestamped result, uses a lock to prevent overlap, and exits non-zero on failure. Schedule it with cron or a systemd timer and verify logs after one successful and one failed run.
